    Resizecurrent · R-STR-003 R-HON-003 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-060
    a resize is not a redraw — three things have to survive it
 
  the SCROLL   by anchor: the top visible entry stays the top
               visible entry, whatever its new height is
  the FOCUS    by id, falling forward to the nearest survivor —
               the element list is a function of width, so the
               element you were on may not exist at 60 columns
  the CARET    by character index, not by column — a rewrapped
               line puts the same character somewhere else
 
  none of the three is a position on screen. All three are
  identities, and the position is recomputed — which is why a resize
  does not feel like losing your place.
 
what a resize is allowed to change
 
  how much is visible, the wrapping, a plot's sample count, a
  table's columns, whether the label on the prompt's rule fits.
 
what it is NOT allowed to change
 
  the scope. A resize while you are inside a block leaves you inside
  it — and if the block lost its rows entirely, you land on the block
  rather than at the prompt.
  
  a resize that dumps you back to the prompt is a resize that made
  you start again.
 
and it coalesces
 
  a drag is thirty events. One frame at the end of the window, not
  thirty — which is measured, not assumed: this tree once spent
  544ms on a 30-event drag before the window was added.
    

    Eight cases that are not edge casescurrent · R-OWN-001 R-OWN-002 R-OWN-003 R-QST-001 R-TXT-001 R-COR-001 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-061
    eight cases that look like edge cases and are not — every one is
something a reader hits by accident on the first afternoon.
 
1 · ORDINARY CONTENT ARRIVES. Three states, three answers.
  at the bottom     follow it. You were reading the end
  scrolled up       DO NOT MOVE. The anchor holds, and the chrome
                    counts what arrived — a button, above the prompt
  navigating        DO NOT MOVE. Focus is a position and a new
                    entry is not a reason to leave it
  an ownership-request event is different: a new question explicitly
  raises its owner and arms it against in-flight input.
  
  one of these three is wrong in most terminal apps, and it is
  always the second: the view yanks to the bottom while you read.
 
2 · TYPING WHILE A CHOICE-ONLY QUESTION IS OPEN
  the prompt is held, so a letter has nowhere to land. But a SILENT
  no-op reads as a frozen app.
  
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 ⟩ Apply this change?     ▲ answer this first                                 
  › no    yes    show full diff                                          
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
←→ move     ⏎ answer   — esc resolves to NO
  
  the first keystroke that is not an answer puts that notice on the
  question, once. It is not an error and it does not repeat.
 
3 · PASTE, IN FOUR PLACES
  the prompt, small    inserted at the caret, as text
  the prompt, large    a chip — [#1 json · 47L] — at the caret
  a text question      into its isolated editor; implementation shared, state separate
  not focused          focus the prompt first, then paste. A paste is
                       a request to type, so it goes where typing goes
  
  and a paste is NEVER submitted by its own newlines — bracketed
  paste exists precisely so a pasted \n is a newline and not a send.
 
4 · ⌃C INSIDE A SUBAGENT CANCELS THAT AGENT
  not all of them, and not the parent. You are looking at one, and
  the frame you are looking at is the one your keys act on.
  
  cancelling the whole fan-out is ⌃C on the PARENT's entry, where
  the head says 3 agents — which is a different place, deliberately.
 
5 · A GRAPHEME IS ONE THING TO THE CARET AND TWO CELLS TO THE SCREEN
  ❯ ship it ⚡ now
  ←→ move ONE index and the caret jumps TWO columns. ⌫ removes the
  whole cluster — never half an emoji, never a lone combining mark.
  
  the same rule the span model takes, one layer down: the unit is
  the cluster and the WIDTH is a separate question.
 
6 · THE WINDOW LOSES FOCUS
  held keys stop repeating. The cursor stops blinking. Spinners and
  ramps keep going, because the work has not stopped.
  
  a held arrow that keeps repeating after you alt-tab away is a
  scroll position you did not choose, and the release event never
  arrives to end it.
 
7 · A FOCUSED BLOCK IS REPLACED OR EVICTED WHILE YOU ARE IN IT
  a streaming block is replaced whole on every patch, and the
  transcript evicts at its cap. Focus resolves BY ID and falls
  forward to the nearest survivor — the same operation a resize and
  focus memory both use.
  
  and if the whole ENTRY went, focus lands on its neighbour rather
  than at the prompt. Being moved is survivable; being ejected is
  not.
 
8 · THE CONNECTION DROPS MID-TURN
  ● The parser tracks quotes with a boolean, so a nes
  
  ─────────  ERROR  ─────────
  ✗ transport closed after 312 tokens
  
   retrying in 8s · attempt 2     2 queued, held
  
  the partial reply STAYS. The queue is HELD rather than dropped or
  sent — and it says so, because a queue that silently fired on
  reconnect is the worst outcome of the three.
 
the thread through all eight
 
  nothing moves the reader without their asking, and no accepted or rejected
  command silently does nothing.
  
  those are the two failures people describe as the app feeling
  broken, and neither of them is a bug in the usual sense.
    

    Latency — and the window that causes itcurrent · R-HON-005 R-HON-003 R-COR-001 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-062
    ★ the coalescing window is also the INPUT LATENCY FLOOR, and that is a
problem the framework created for itself
 
  C03 coalesces commits into one frame per 100ms window. That is what
  makes a streaming turn affordable — and it means a keystroke can
  wait up to 100ms to appear.
  
  100ms is the number at which a person stops believing they caused
  the thing. So typing at the window's rate feels like a bad ssh
  connection on a local machine.
 
so input does not go through the window
 
  a keystroke that only changes the PROMPT   draw now
  a keystroke that moves FOCUS               draw now
  a keystroke that changes the DOCUMENT      the window
  a stream patch                             the window
  a tick                                     the window
  
  the split is not urgency, it is CAUSATION: a reader pressed a key
  and is waiting to see it. Everything else arrived on its own and
  nobody is watching for it at 16ms.
 
  and the cost is bounded, because a person types at ten a second
  and a stream arrives at ninety. Exempting input exempts the SMALL
  population.
 
three framework budgets, plus an unbounded turn
 
  echo        ≤ 16ms    slower and typing feels laggy
  a key that  ≤ 50ms    slower and the arrows feel sticky
  moves focus           
  a frame     ≤ 16ms    slower and a stream stutters
  a turn      no budget it takes what it takes, and the
                        elapsed counter is the honest answer
 
  only the first three are the framework's. Confusing them with the
  fourth is how a tool ends up feeling slow while every number in
  it is green.
    

    Three refusals, and what stays rebindablecurrent · R-REF-001 R-REF-002 R-REF-003 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-063
    three things refused, and each is refused for the same reason
 
1 · NO LEADER KEYS, NO TWO-KEY SEQUENCES [R-REF-001]
  no ⌃x ⌃s, no g g, no space-then-f. A sequence is a MODE you are
  in for 400ms without being told — and the way you discover you
  were in it is that the next key did something else.
  
  every binding is one chord. The footer shows the highest-ranked live
  actions that fit; help shows all. A sequence cannot be shown; it can only be
  remembered.
 
2 · NO CHORDS THE PLATFORM ALREADY OWNS [R-REF-002]
  ⌥←→ is word movement. ⌘←→ is line ends. ⌘C is the terminal's
  copy. ⌃↑ is Mission Control. Taking one wins an argument with the
  reader's own machine, and the machine wins.
 
3 · NO KEY THAT ONLY WORKS SOMETIMES [R-REF-003]
  if ⏎ means open in the transcript, it opens in EVERY scope that
  has something to open, and it is absent from the footer where it
  does not. A key that silently does nothing in one place is worse
  than a key that does not exist.
 
and what is deliberately left rebindable
 
  every chord is rebindable. Confirm, safe exit, focus movement and
  interrupt are structural ACTIONS, so each must keep one reachable
  binding or named-command path after conflict resolution.
  
  ❯ /keys posture ⌥p
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 ⟩ ⌥p is already cycle posture. Replace it?                                   
  › no    replace it    pick another chord                                    
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
←→ move     ⏎ answer   — a conflict is a QUESTION like any other
  › no    replace it    pick another chord                                    
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
←→ move     ⏎ answer   — a conflict is a QUESTION like any other
  
  a conflict is answered before it is written, not discovered when
  the old binding stops working.
 
prompt undo is the editor's, not the agent's
 
  ⌘Z        undo in the line editor — your typing only
  ⌘⇧Z       redo
  ↺ on an entry  revert what the AGENT did — a different thing,
                in a different place, with a different key
  
  sharing one undo between the two would mean ⌘Z sometimes touches
  your files, which is the kind of surprise nobody recovers trust
  from.
    

    Undocurrent · R-QST-003 R-HON-007 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-064
    undo is a transcript entry, because an invisible undo is one you do
twice
 
● edit(parse.ts) · 0.3s · +2 −2
 
● reverted · parse.ts · +2 −2 undone   ↺ redo
  ⎿ the file is back to what it was before the edit above
 
it is muted, because nothing went wrong and nothing is pending — it
is a fact about history, and history is what the transcript IS.
 
what can be undone, and what cannot
 
  an edit the agent made    yes — the patch is the record
  a whole turn's edits      yes — the review row's ↺ revert all
  a command it ran          NO. rm does not come back, and offering
                            an undo that cannot work is worse than
                            having none
  your own message          only while it is queued — ⌥⌫
 
  so the affordance appears where it is TRUE and nowhere else. A
  greyed-out undo teaches people to stop looking for it.
    

    Compaction — which turns gocurrent · R-COR-001 R-HON-007 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-065
    the context fills, and a harness can say WHICH TURNS GO — a statusline cannot
 
  ctx ██████████████████████████████░░  94%   ⏎ breakdown
 
  ▲ the next turn drops 3 turns
    turn 4   read_file(construct.ts)      8.1k tok
    turn 5   search("elementsIn")         2.2k tok
    turn 6   your question about spans    0.4k tok
    ⏎ summarise instead   p pin a turn   esc let it drop
 
you are at 94% is a WARNING. These three turns drop when you send this
is a DECISION — and only a harness holds the turns to say it.
 
after compaction the transcript says so, in place
 
   compacting   ▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▱▱▱▱▱▱▱▱▱▱  3 of 5 turns
  
  ● 3 turns compacted · 10.7k → 0.9k tok · ⏎ read the summary
  ⎿ read construct.ts, searched for elementsIn, discussed the span
    prerequisite. No edits were made.
 
  it is an ENTRY, not a gap — because a conversation that silently
  forgets is one you cannot reason about.
    

    Tool failures against model failurescurrent · R-COL-001 R-HON-004 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-066
    a tool failed and the MODEL failed are different facts, and the shapes differ
 
a TOOL failure is a result — it hangs under its own call and the turn goes on
  ● read_file(missing.ts) · 0.1s · failed
    ⎿ ✗ ENOENT: no such file
  ● I'll check the directory listing instead.     ← the turn continues
 
a MODEL failure ends the turn, and it is the status block
  ● The parser tracks quotes with a boolean, so a nes
  
  ──────────  ERROR  ──────────
  ✗ context exhausted at 50,000 tokens
  
   retrying in 8s · attempt 2        ← and it retries, visibly
 
four model failures, four answers
 
  rate limited      retry with backoff, and SAY the wait
  context exhausted offer compaction — it is actionable
  refused           not an error. The model answered
  transport died    the status block, and the partial reply STAYS
 
  a refusal is the model's answer and gets no error treatment:
  ● I won't do that — here is why, and what I can do instead.
 
  conflating the two teaches a reader to ignore red.
    

    Scrolled back while a turn runscurrent · R-COR-001 R-INT-008 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-067
    the activity line is the RUNNING ENTRY'S HEAD, so it lives in the
transcript and it scrolls. It is not chrome.
 
  calcium   ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high        localhost:8000   22:18
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 ❯ what does elementsIn actually walk?                                        
 
  ● It walks the entry's blocks depth-first, and only a kind that
    declares elements contributes any.
 
    editing parse.ts  41s · 3.2k tok
  ⎿ todo  4/5  ·  ◻ run the suite
 
   ↓ 3 new messages ⏎  
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ❯ ▌
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  » auto   ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high            localhost:8000   22:13
  ███████████████████░░░░░  78%  39k/50k   step ███████░░░ 7/10   28 tok/s
  ~/code/calcium   ⎇ feat/c26   +124/-18 ~1   ✎ 3          malachy   31m
 
★ the activity line SCROLLS — it is part of the transcript
 
  it is the head of the entry being written. An entry that floated
  free of the record while it was running and then dropped into it
  when it settled would be two objects wearing one shape.
  
  so scrolling up CAN take it off screen, and that is correct: you
  went to read something else.
 
what stays visible instead, and it is enough
 
  » auto   ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high            localhost:8000   22:13
  ███████████████████░░░░░  78%  39k/50k   step ███████░░░ 7/10   28 tok/s
  ~/code/calcium   ⎇ feat/c26   +124/-18 ~1   ✎ 3          malachy   31m
  the STEP count says how far through, the CONTEXT bar says how full,
  the TOKEN rate says it is still producing. Three live numbers, in
  the one place this document already puts live state.
  
  a fourth copy of what the agent is doing, pinned above the prompt,
  would be the activity line said twice — and the second one could not
  be scrolled to, copied, or expanded.
 
★ the notice sits DIRECTLY ABOVE THE PROMPT, and it is a BUTTON
 
  it is not chrome and not a status line. It is the thing you would
  reach for, so it sits where your hand already is — one row above the
  prompt.
  
  AT REST it is bgElev, like every other button. It is not active and
  nothing is waiting on it, so it does not wear the accent — that is
  reserved for the thing you are ON.
  
  and the ⏎ is INSIDE the button, because it is the button's own key
  rather than a hint about the frame. A key printed beside a control is
  a caption; a key printed on it is a label.
  
  clicking it does the same thing, because every consumed gesture lands on a
  state a key reaches.
 
★ and it counts MESSAGES, not rows
 
   ↓ 3 new messages ⏎    a reader knows what a message is
   ↓ 214 rows below      nobody has ever wanted this number
  
  a row is a rendering fact — it changes with the width, with a table's
  columns, with whether a block is expanded. 214 rows is 3 messages at
  one width and 340 at another, and the reader has not missed any more
  of the conversation for being in a narrow terminal.
  
  and a MESSAGE is what they are counting when they ask what they
  missed — so that is the number the chrome owes them.
 
what counts as one
 
  a settled entry     yes — a reply, a call, a patch, an agent fan-out
  the running entry   NO. It has not arrived yet, and it is visible
                      in the activity region anyway
  a patch to a block  NO. The entry was already counted
  your own message    NO. You just sent it
 
  so the count is entries that SETTLED while you were scrolled away —
  which is exactly the set you would have to scroll back to read.
 
the three states it takes
 
   ↓ 3 new messages ⏎       at rest
   ↓ 1 new message ⏎        singular, because 1 messages is sloppy
   ↓ 3 new messages ⏎       hovered — preview, no focus carrier
   › ↓ 3 new messages ⏎     focused — mark and edge persist
                          scrolled up, nothing new — NOTHING is drawn
 
  scrolled up with nothing new needs no notice. A button that says
  nothing happened is a row spent on nothing, and ⌘↓ is already there.
 
a new entry does NOT move a scrolled-up reader — the anchor holds, and the
button is how they know something arrived.
 
  which is the whole arrangement: the TRANSCRIPT is the record and it
  all scrolls, the FOOTER is live state and it never moves, and the
  BUTTON is the one thing that bridges them.

    /colour — tinting the chromecurrent · R-COL-001 R-COL-002 R-COL-003 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-070
    /colour takes a COLOUR NAME — not a tone. The tones mean something;
this is you choosing what your terminal looks like.
 
   blue   orange   cyan   pink   lime   violet   yellow   green   red   purple  
 
ten hues, VIVID — they are the point, not a tint of the theme. The ink
on each is chosen by CONTRAST against that hue, so yellow takes black
and blue takes white without anyone deciding per theme.
 
solid — the default
 
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── calcium ─
❯ /colour blue
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── prod ─
❯ /colour red                             the one you must not break
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── scratch ─
❯ /colour lime
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
a gradient — built in, or two hues
 
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── calcium ─
❯ /colour viridis                         any colormap the plot system has
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── calcium ─
❯ /colour blue..pink                      two hues, interpolated
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
animated — the same ramps, on a rule
 
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── calcium ─
❯ /colour cyan --animate wave
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── calcium ─
❯ /colour purple --animate drift
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
  ▲ available, and a bad default — a rule that moves is motion with
  nothing behind it. This is an explicit PERSONALIZATION/DECORATION exception:
  default off, never semantic, and suppressed in REDUCED and OFF.
 
a hex — and this is where the rule changes
 
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── calcium ─
❯ /colour #e07aa8                         taken literally
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 
  everywhere else in this system a hex is refused, because C10 owns
  colour and a literal cannot follow a theme change.
 
  HERE THAT IS THE POINT. You are picking a colour to tell this
  terminal apart, and one that shifted when you changed theme would
  be broken from where you are standing.
 
  so: a NAME resolves per theme and stays legible. A HEX is taken
  as given and you own the result — with one check.
 
and the check is a CHOICE-ONLY question, so it normally replaces the prompt.
It is never a line of prose with two unowned words after it.
 
● read_file(parse.ts) · 0.2s · 184 lines
 
 
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 ⟩ Set this colour?                                                           
                                                                              
 #2a2a2a is 1.4:1 against this theme's ground.                                
 It will be invisible on Ink and on High contrast.                            
                                                                              
  › no    yes, set it anyway    pick from the ten                             
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
←→ move     ⏎ answer   — esc resolves to NO
 
  the safe answer is initially focused, esc resolves to it, and the third
  choice is the way out — the same three rules every choice-only safety question takes.
 
what it is actually for
 
  one terminal is not one project. Four windows on four checkouts
  look identical, and the cost of typing into the wrong one is a
  bad afternoon.
 
  a painted label is the cheapest answer: zero rows, one glance,
  and it sits where your eye already is when you type.
 
two rules that survive
 
  it persists per directory, in .calcium/config.toml — the point is
  that THIS checkout looks like this
  
  chrome only. A painted label is furniture; a painted transcript is
  a theme, and that is a different command
 
  /colour                 open the picker
  /colour blue            a hue
  /colour blue..pink      a gradient between two
  /colour viridis         a colormap
  /colour #e07aa8         a literal, checked for contrast
  /colour cyan --animate  wave · drift · breathe · shimmer
  /colour off             back to the default
  /label prod             the label is its own verb
    

    The five permission posturescurrent · R-PER-001 R-COL-001 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-071
    five postures, five symbols — and NOT ONE of them is painted
 
  ❯ manual           grey    every call comes back to you — the prompt's own chevron
  ? accept-edits    purple  edits go; it still asks about commands
  ❙❙ plan          blue    nothing is written
  » auto             yellow  nothing asks — fast forward
  !! skip             red     no permission check at all
 
why none of them is painted, and it is the whole answer to the error problem
 
  THE ERROR TAG IS THE ONLY PAINTED LABEL THAT MEANS A STATUS.
    ────────  ERROR  ────────
  so a posture drawn in text can never be mistaken for one, however red
  it is. The distinction is the CHANNEL, not the hue — which is stronger
  than any amount of picking different reds.
 
  and skip does not flash. It is not asking for your attention every
  second — it is telling you what is true, once.
 
the footer, in each posture
 
  ❯ manual   ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high       localhost:8000
  ? accept-edits ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high       localhost:8000
  ❙❙ plan     ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high       localhost:8000
  » auto     ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high       localhost:8000
  !! skip     ✦ qwen3-coder-next   effort high       no permission checks
 
  skip earns its loudness with a CLAUSE, not a colour — the thing it
  adds is the sentence at the end of the line.
 
the symbols, every one measured before it was picked
 
  ❯    U+276F   narrow, no emoji form    the prompt's own mark
  ?    U+003F   ascii                   it still asks
  ❙❙   U+2759   narrow, no emoji form    ⏸ U+23F8 IS an emoji — the ⏺ trap again
  »    U+00BB   narrow                   fast forward
  !!   U+0021   ascii                   the only ASCII symbol, for the only
                                        posture that is a warning to YOU
 
  ‼ U+203C is an emoji and ⚡ is wide AND an emoji. Two plain
  exclamation marks need no table at all.
 
  ascii    > manual   ? accept   || plan   >> auto   !! skip
 
and every one survives to 1-bit, where no tone is left
  ❯ manual   ? accept-edits   ❙❙ plan   » auto   !! skip
    

    The background is a second channelcurrent · R-COL-003 R-COL-004 R-STA-002 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-072
    a background is for an EXTENT. a foreground is for a MARK.
something with length or area takes a ground; a symbol or a label does not.
 
1 · a changed line — and the ground runs to the BLOCK'S EDGE, not the text's
     41 - let inQuote = false;                                 
     41 + let depth = 0;                                       
     47 - if (ch === '"') inQuote = !inQuote;                  
     47 + if (ch === '"') depth += (ch === q) ? (esc ? 0 : 1) : 0;         
     52   return tokens;
    the LINE changed, so the line is painted. A ground stopping at the
    last character says a word changed, which is a different claim.
 
2 · a word-level change inside an unchanged line — now the ground is short
     63   const rows = measureSequence(blocks, width);
     63   const rows = measureWindow(blocks, width);
    the extent IS the claim — and this needs spans, which is why it is
    the substrate arc's subject rather than a rendering choice.
 
3 · a TAG with extent — and the error tag is the only one in the system
     ERROR          a failure, and only a failure
    » auto          a posture — TEXT, never a ground
    so a posture can never be mistaken for an error, whatever its hue
 
4 · a context bar — the segments are grounds, so the composition is legible
    ctx                                 78%   ⏎ breakdown
        └sys─┘└tool┘└─turns──┘└file┘
    one read_file swallowed about 23% and it is visible, not an unexplained jump
 
5 · a selection — a run the terminal cannot tell you the bounds of
    explain this error and compare with the previous run
 
6 · a focused row — a wash plus a persistent mark
      a3f9b21  digit-classifier  running    0.0372   23m
    ▸ 7c2d4e1  decoder-zoom      succeeded  0.0089   41m  
      2e8a04c  graphsage         failed     —        1h
 
7 · a value's magnitude in a table cell — the ground IS the number
    gpu-01  ░░▒▒▒▒▓▓██▓▓▒▒░░   71%
    gpu-02  ░░░░▒▒▒▒▒▒░░░░░░   34%
    a sparkline says the shape. A painted cell says the LEVEL, and both
    fit in a column a number would need eight of.
 
8 · a half-block image — two full colours per cell, the one place a ground
    doubles the resolution rather than decorating it
    ▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀   fg = the top pixel, bg = the bottom; metadata is the nonvisual equivalent
 
9 · a well — structural, never semantic. bgDeep says CONTENT INSIDE
     loss                                          
     4.0┤⢀⡠⠔⠒⠉⠉⠑⠒⠢⢄                        
     0.0┼──────────────────────────────────────────
 
the two rules
 
  structural grounds and semantic grounds never mix. A panel takes bgElev;
  it never takes diffAdd. A well is bgDeep; a selection is not.
 
  and a ground is NEVER the only carrier for actionable/status state — surfaces vanish at 1-bit:
     41 - let inQuote = false;     the +/− carries it
    ▸ 7c2d4e1  decoder-zoom        the ▸ carries it
    » auto                        the » and the bold carry it
    

    Painted chrome — buttons, titles, widgets, headerscurrent · R-COL-003 R-COL-005 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-073
    the error tag is the only painted thing that means a STATUS. Everything
below is painted because it is a SURFACE — a thing you act on or a thing
that holds other things. Different job, no confusion.
 
buttons — four states, and the ground is the affordance
 
   Approve    Deny         resting
   › Approve    Deny       focused — ⏎ activates
   Approve    Deny         a destructive pair takes tone:
   Approve    Deny         green to go, red to stop
   Approve    Deny         disabled — a WELL, not a button
  [ Approve ]  [ Deny ]       1-bit and ascii — brackets carry it
 
titles — three treatments, and each says something different
 
   workers ──────────────────────────────────────     painted — a NAMED region
  ┌ containers ────────────────────────────────────┐   inset — the default, cheapest
  containers  ──────────────────────────────────────       bare — a heading, not a container
 
   running  3 ──────────────────────────────────────   a title that carries a STATE
   degraded  1 ────────────────────────────────────  and a count beside it
 
widgets — the ground is the track, the glyph is the value
 
  learning rate        ●          3e-4
                 ├──────●────────┤  3e-4    the glyph rung
 
  mode            ✓ linear  log  log₂      segmented — the chosen
                 ( ) linear  (●) log  ( ) log₂     segment is the painted one
 
  live            ✓ on            a switch is ON when painted
                  off ○            and a well when it is not
 
  series          ✓ train   ✓ val   test   on / on / off
 
a table header — the one place a full-width ground is right
 
   uuid     family            status     metric   age 
  ▸ ● a3f9b21  digit-classifier  running    0.0372   23m
    ✓ 7c2d4e1  decoder-zoom      succeeded  0.0089   41m
  it is a SURFACE the rows sit under, not a status — and it makes the
  column names stop competing with the data for the eye.
 
what must never be painted
 
  a status word          running  not  running 
  a permission posture   » auto   a posture is text
  body text              anything you read at length
  a whole block          a wash over content is a MODE, and there is none
 
  the test: am I painting a THING (a button, a track, a header) or a
  FACT about a thing (its status, its mode, its outcome)?
  Things take a ground. Facts take a tone.
    

    Weight, and why it is not freecurrent · R-COR-003 R-COL-002 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-074
    bold works, and it is SGR 1 — as old and as universal as colour itself
 
  ␛[1m  bold        bold text            universal
  ␛[2m  dim         dim text             widely supported, sometimes ignored
  ␛[3m  italic      italic text          common, not universal
  ␛[4m  underline   underlined text      universal
  ␛[7m  inverse      inverse text        universal, and it is 1-bit's ground
 
but weight is NOT a free axis here — it is already bound to tone
 
  ok · warn · error · accent · identifier  emphasised → bold at 1-bit
  default · info · meta        normal         → plain
  dim · muted                deemphasised   → faint at 1-bit
  
  syntax roles resolve first: syntax.keyword → bold; every other syntax
  slot → plain. Generic ok, warn and meta aliases do not override syntax.
 
  so at 1-bit, where every colour is gone, the TONE STILL READS —
  because it was never only a colour:
 
  24-bit   ● a3f9b21  succeeded      ● b81c003  failed
  1-bit    ● a3f9b21  succeeded      ✗ b81c003  failed
           the mark separates them where the weight cannot
 
which is why bold is not available as decoration
  bolding a muted label contradicts its own tone — the theme says
  deemphasised and the render says look here.
    

    /config — and where a value came fromcurrent · R-HON-008 R-PER-001 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-075
    /config — and the third column is the one that matters
 
┌ config ──────────────────── ~/.calcium/config.toml ────────────────────────┐
│  key                    value              source       
│ ▸ model                  qwen3-coder-next   config      
│   endpoint               localhost:8000     env         
│   posture                auto               flag        
│   effort                 high               config      
│   ui.theme               ink                config      
│   ui.colour              blue               config      
│   ui.spinner             braille            default     
│   context.cap            50000              default     
│                                                                        
└ ⏎ edit   r reset to default   esc back   ──────────────────────────────────────┘
 
four sources, and the tone is the ladder — the later it is applied, the
louder it is, because a flag beating your config file is the thing you
forget you did.
 
  default   the framework's                 muted — nobody chose it
  config    ~/.calcium/config.toml         meta — you chose it
  env       CALCIUM_ENDPOINT             warn — your shell chose it
  flag      --posture auto                error — this invocation chose it
 
a config view without a source column is one you cannot debug — the
commonest question is not what is it, it is WHY is it that.
 
and it is per-directory as well as global
  ~/.calcium/config.toml         the account's
  ./.calcium/config.toml         this checkout's — and it wins
  which is where /colour and /label write, so a project keeps its
  own chrome without anyone editing a file.
    

    Per-token valuescurrent · R-TXT-001 R-COL-002 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-076
    per-token values over the model's own output — the case that extends
the shared run/span mechanism with numeric values
 
  The parser tracks quotes with a boolean.
  low  ░▒▓█  high                       per-token probability
 
the unit is a TOKEN IN WRAPPED PROSE — not a row, not a cell. So table
cannot hold it, a span carries appearance and not a value, and every
plot form is axis-based.
 
three things it needs
 
  a per-token VALUE        driving a ground, or a mark beneath
  tokens survive wrapping  a token near a line end wraps whole
  selection by token       ⇧←→ extends by token, not by grapheme
 
and it is the SAME mechanism spans needed — inline emphasis wanted a
STYLED run and this wants a VALUED one. The symbol is reserved.
 
where it earns its place in an agent surface
 
  the model hedged here    a low-confidence run is visible, not buried
  which tokens cost        an expensive rewrite has a shape
  what came from the tool  quoted context against generated text
 
  ▲ and it is off by default. A wall of shaded prose is harder to
  read than prose, and the value is a diagnostic rather than a
  reading — ⌥v toggles it on the entry under the cursor.
    

    Syntax highlightingcurrent · R-COL-001 R-COL-002 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-077
    the syntax palette — six slots, and they are TONES rather than a second
set of colours
 
  keyword     meta        const, if, return, function
  string      ok          a literal, and it reads as data
  number      warn        including a boolean — a value, not a name
  identifier  identifier  a name you or the code chose
  comment     muted       furniture, and it recedes
  everything  default     punctuation, operators, whitespace
 
  export function parse(src: string): Token[] {
    const out = [];            // the accumulator
    let depth = 0;
    if (ch === '"') depth += depth > 0 ? -1 : 1;
 
six slots because six is what a reader can hold. Twenty-slot themes
exist and nobody can name what the twentieth means — they are chosen
for coverage, not for reading.
 
★ and it borrows the SAME tones the rest of the system uses
 
  which means a theme has one palette rather than two, and a reader
  who has learnt that identifier tone means A NAME learns nothing
  new when they look at code.
  
  it also means a syntax colour can never contradict a status one:
  there is no separate red for an error in code, because errors are
  not a syntax category.
 
where it applies, and where it does not
 
  a code block          yes
  a patch, ALL THREE kinds yes — removed lines too
  a tool's arguments    yes — they are code
  the prompt            only a leading /command, and only the verb
  agent prose           no — it is prose, and inline ` ` is a span
 
degradation
 
  8-bit · 4-bit  the same six, quantised

    Prism — the rework in one sentencecurrent · R-STR-001 R-PRG-001 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-080
    the rework, in one sentence: a Prism command is a CALL.
 
BEFORE — every command produced a bespoke framed panel with its own
gutter, its own rules, its own header, its own footer hints.
  ▌ ── ps · 4 of 11 · --mine · last 24h ───────────────────
  ▌
  ▌   uuid     family          status
  ▌ ▸ a3f9b21  digit-classif…  running
  ▌
  ▌ ⏎ detail  ␣ expand  ≡ logs
 
AFTER — the call grammar, which every surface already uses
  ● ps --mine --since 24h · 0.3s · 4 of 11
    ⎿  uuid     family            status      metric   age 
       a3f9b21  digit-classifier  running     0.0372    23m 
       7c2d4e1  decoder-zoom      succeeded   0.0089    41m 
       2e8a04c  graphsage         failed           —   1h12m 
       f410d99  flow-predictor    queued            —      3m 
 
what that one change buys
 
  the ▌ gutter, the panel rules, the per-surface footer hint and the
  bespoke header are all GONE — four pieces of chrome per surface,
  across fifteen surfaces.
  
  the result-summary slot now says 4 of 11 where the old header said it,
  and it says it in the same place every other call does.
  
  the table is bounded and windowed like any block, so a 400-run
  list is eight rows and a residue — which the panel version had to
  solve for itself.
  
  and the keys are the FRAMEWORK's: ⇥ to it, ↑↓ the rows, ⏎ opens,
  ⌃⇧C copies the values. No surface teaches its own.
 
  ▲ and it makes Prism and the agent ONE product rather than two
  sharing a renderer — a /ps result and a read_file result are the
  same object with different contents, which is what §1 claimed all
  along and the old surfaces quietly contradicted.

    No pushed viewscurrent · R-INT-001 R-INT-008 · retained example blocks generated from registry · example R-EXA-082
    ★ THERE ARE NO PUSHED VIEWS. Correcting an earlier pass.
 
a pushed view takes the screen, you do something, you come back — and
the transcript has a HOLE where that work was. The record is the
product here, and a surface that steps outside it is a surface whose
output you cannot scroll back to.
 
three surfaces, and a push is not one of them
 
  THE TRANSCRIPT  everything that HAPPENED. It is the record, and
                  work belongs in it
  A QUESTION      an ownership request. It resolves once and never
                  holds work; panel / peek / overlay describe its layer
  A TAB           a PARALLEL document with its own prompt and its
                  own context. ⌃⇥, like a browser
 
what each thing I had pushed becomes instead
 
  a run's detail    →  EXPANDS IN PLACE. ⏎ on the row, and the
                       detail unfolds under it
  logs              →  A BLOCK with follow. It was already a
                       scroll container; it needed no frame
  the help view     →  AN ENTRY. ? emits the keymap, and it is in
                       your scrollback, copyable, scrolled past
  an attached PTY   →  A CAPTURED CHILD OWNER over its block. The border says your
                       keys go to the child; the transcript stays
  a subagent        →  A TAB, which it already was — ⌃⇥ is what
                       tabs use, and a tab is not a push
 
  the subagent is the only one that LOOKS like a push and is not: it
  is a second conversation with its own context window and its own
  prompt. You SWITCH to it and it is still there when you switch
  back. Nothing was hidden and nothing was lost.
 
the test, when something wants a frame of its own
 
  does it have its own PROMPT and its own CONTEXT?
    yes — it is a tab
    no  — it is a block, or an entry, or a question
  
  everything I pushed answered NO, which is how I know the earlier
  pass was wrong rather than merely different.
 
and what an expanded entry looks like — which is most of the answer
 
● ps · 0.3s · 2 of 11
  ⎿  uuid     family            status      metric   age 
    ▸ ▾ a3f9b21  digit-classifier  running     0.0372   23m 
        node   gpu-04.fmx.internal · 2×A100 · 16GiB      
        mr     !1248  auto-merged                      
        ██████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  43%  ep 17/40  ~18m    
        ≡ logs  ⚡ events  ⊘ cancel  { } json           
      7c2d4e1  decoder-zoom      succeeded   0.0089   41m

▸ keeps focus while ▾ independently says expanded. The detail sits on bgElev — the
inside ground, which is the same one block scope already uses — and
the rows below carry on underneath.
 
  you can see the run you opened AND the one you were comparing it
  to. A pushed view could not show you both, which is the whole
  reason this is better.

and THAT is the point: the logs are still on screen while you ask
